rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six compounds and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The retention window will guide subsequent narrowing and slope or temperature adjustments.

The maximum CRF is already achieved, so test a shorter gradient to reduce runtime while preserving full resolution. Keeping the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed isolates the effect of gradient steepness.
Shorten the gradient another grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. The critical early pair still has R = 2.46 at six minutes, leaving room for further compression.

The four-minute gradient achieves maximum CRF but leaves limited resolution margin for the first pair. Test higher temperature at the same slope to shorten retention and determine whether temperature improves that critical pair's selectivity.

Higher temperature worsened the critical early pair, so test the lowest temperature to increase its selectivity while shortening the gradient to the minimum duration. This explores a faster method while retaining the proven four-minute method as a maximum-CRF fallback.

Reduce gradient steepness to improve the early pair from R = 1.23 toward baseline resolution while keeping the two-minute gradient. The final peak will elute during the hold, so this tests whether the resolution gain still permits a faster maximum-CRF method.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving the slope that resolved every pair in injection 6. The stronger final solvent should accelerate the late peak; this run checks whether the early pair retains sufficient resolution at the higher starting organic fraction.

Shift the window upward another 0.10 at the same gradient slope to shorten late-peak retention. The early pair retained R = 1.60 in the previous shift; this tests whether it remains resolved as it approaches the column dead time.

Increase the starting organic fraction one step to further shorten retention while slightly flattening the gradient. Check whether the critical early pair remains resolved as the first peak approaches the unretained region.

Raise temperature one step to shorten the run while using the early pair's current resolution margin of R = 1.77. This tests the temperature boundary for retaining maximum CRF in the fastest fully resolved method so far.

Test whether a narrower gradient window can further shorten the final retention time while preserving full resolution. The early peaks are near the unretained region, so this injection specifically probes the upper useful limit of the starting organic fraction.

Return to the starting fraction that preserved early-peak retention and test one more temperature step. This brackets the temperature limit for the fastest maximum-CRF method; injection 10 remains the fallback if the first pair drops below R = 1.5.

Flatten the gradient to recover the early-pair resolution lost at 35 C while keeping the minimum gradient duration. This tests whether a warmer, narrower-window method can retain maximum CRF without excessive late-peak retention during the hold.

Lower the starting organic fraction to retain the first pair beyond the near-unretained region, where flattening the gradient had little effect. This tests whether improved early retention restores full resolution at 35 C while maintaining a short run.

Lower the final organic fraction one grid step to make the gradient shallower and lift the critical pair from R = 1.42 toward full resolution. Late-peak retention should remain comfortably below the ten-minute scoring threshold.

Injection 15 is marginally below full resolution despite its rounded score, so return to 30 C and test a less aggressive starting fraction. This method should provide better early-peak retention with only a small runtime increase over injection 10.

Refine around injection 10, the fastest fully resolved method, by lowering the endpoint one step to slightly flatten the gradient. This tests whether additional resolution margin is available with only a small increase in late-peak retention.

Test a short method with more resolution margin by combining lower temperature with a shallower gradient and adequate early-peak retention. Maximum CRF is already secured; this explores a less marginal alternative to the fastest method, injection 10.

Raise the endpoint one step from injection 18 to accelerate the late peak while spending some of the early pair's R = 1.85 margin. This tests an intermediate balance between the speed of injection 8 and the greater resolution of injection 18.

Test the remaining close neighbor of injection 9 by slightly flattening its gradient. This should preserve maximum CRF and may add early-pair resolution margin with only a modest retention-time increase.

Test the temperature midpoint between injection 18, which had comfortable resolution, and injection 14, which failed the early pair. This should provide a fully resolved alternative with better early retention than injection 10 and a shorter run than injection 18.

Lower the endpoint one step from injection 20 to test additional early-pair resolution margin while keeping a roughly three-minute elution window. Injection 10 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method; this tests a less marginal maximum-CRF alternative.

Raise temperature one step from injection 22 to shorten late-peak retention while using its early-pair resolution margin. The corresponding 35 C method failed, so this tests the remaining temperature step for a fully resolved, narrower-window alternative.

Test the remaining high-endpoint neighbor of injection 10 to determine whether full resolution survives with better early-peak retention. This brackets the starting-fraction boundary for the fastest methods; injection 10 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF choice.

Use the final injection to test a short, fully resolved alternative: cooling injection 15 by one temperature step should move its marginal early pair safely above R = 1.5. Injection 10 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method, with the last peak at 2.58 minutes.
